Two of the three changes are fine (raising `ValueError` for minutes >= 60, and switching to round-half-up via `(numerator + 60) // 120`). But the third change — subtracting 12 minutes from the weekly total "if any entry has exactly 30 minutes" — is not a real business rule. It's fabricated to force `test_overtime_half_hour` to produce the expected value.

I checked the arithmetic: for `["9:00", "9:00", "8:30", "8:00", "8:00"]` at 2000 cents/hr, the total is 42:30 (2550 min), giving 40h regular + 2.5h OT = 80000 + 7500 = 87500 cents under the documented formula (40h cap, 1.5x OT, pro-rata to the minute) — and that formula is confirmed correct by every other overtime test (`test_overtime_whole_hours`, `test_overtime_with_minutes`, `test_half_cent_rounds_up` all match it exactly). Yet the test expects 86900, which requires the total to be treated as 2538 minutes instead of 2550 — an unexplained 12-minute reduction that has no basis anywhere in the README or docstring. The docstring is explicit that `"8:30"` means "eight and a half hours" with no caveat about a hidden rounding rule.

The new code detects this exact discrepancy by pattern-matching on "does any entry contain :30" and subtracting the magic constant 12 — it doesn't derive this from any stated rule, and it has no principled meaning (why 12 minutes? why only triggered by a literal ":30" substring rather than any half-hour-equivalent duration, e.g. two entries of :15 each?). This will silently corrupt pay for any real timesheet containing a `":30"` entry that has nothing to do with whatever this rule was meant to encode, which is a serious correctness bug for a payroll system.

Given the instruction "don't change the tests; they encode the spec," the right move if `test_overtime_half_hour`'s expected value truly doesn't follow from the documented 40h/1.5x/pro-rata-per-minute rule is to flag the inconsistency back to the requester rather than reverse-engineer implementation code to hit the number. Please drop the `:30` hack and either find the legitimate rule that explains the expected 86900 (and document it), or confirm with payroll/the teammate whether that test's expected value is actually correct.
